title: Hands left open
hookLine: a woman at a stranger's door, hands held out, asking God that nothing be put in them: Akka Mahadevi's strangest request
carry: a sharana takes refuge in God alone
last: ANUBHAVA: GOD KNOWN BY EXPERIENCE, NOT RANK.

cards: A woman goes from house to house with her hands held out, a wandering seeker begging for her food. What's strange is what she asks for. She doesn't ask God to soften the hearts behind the doors.
She asks for the doors to give her nothing. If they do give, she asks for the food to fall. And if it falls, something stranger still.
Our last day with Akka Mahadevi: one short poem, and a request that runs backward.

teach.b: Here is the vachana, in paraphrase. Make me go from house to house, hands held out for alms. If I beg, let them give me nothing.
If they give, let it fall to the ground. If it falls, before I can pick it up, let a dog come and take it, O lord white as jasmine.

It works like a staircase going down. Each line takes away one more thing to lean on: the comfort of home, the kindness of strangers, the food already in her hand, even the chance to stoop and pick it up.
At the bottom there's nothing left to hold, and the last words are his name. The poem doesn't end on the dog. It ends on the lord white as jasmine.

Her tradition, the Lingayat or Virashaiva way of Karnataka, calls its saints sharanas: those who have taken refuge, in Shiva alone. This poem is that word lived all the way down, every support stripped away but one.
Some readers also hear honesty: she knows how easily a full plate becomes the thing she trusts. So she asks to be emptied, all the way, until the only thing in her hands is him.
The poem never says she starves, and it never asks anyone else to live this way. And there's a small surprise at the bottom of the stairs. A hungry dog eats.
Three days with Akka: a silkworm caught in its own threads, a hard question at the door of the saints, and a woman asking for her hands to stay open.

how: In Karnataka, Akka Mahadevi is honored among the Lingayat (Virashaiva) saints, and her vachanas are sung, recited and taught in Kannada.

o: a Kannada poet-saint who sang to the lord white as jasmine
a goddess of the harvest honored in Karnataka villages
a queen of Karnataka who ruled from the palace at Kalyana

games.q: you're Akka in the poem. someone has given you food, and it slips from your hands to the ground. what do you ask for?
o: to pick it up quickly before it's spoiled.
for a dog to take it before you can.
for the house to give you more.
games.why: she asks for a dog to take it first. even the chance to stoop is given up, and the poem ends on the lord white as jasmine.

practice: Let your hands rest in your lap, palms up and empty. Bring to mind one thing you lean on to feel steady, a plan, someone's approval, a number in an account, a good night's sleep, and just notice how tightly you hold it.
With each breath out, let your palms soften a little more; if you pray, let the open hands be your prayer, without words.

wordCard.voice: Akka Mahadevi. The poet who asked for her alms to fall and a dog to take them, ending on the lord white as jasmine. Today's word.

orig.note: Kannada, the language she sang in. the name she is known by in her own tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: a sharana takes refuge in God alone. Akka asked to be emptied, and ended on his name. Until tomorrow.
